newsitem.title: FRANCE: Recent dollar rise not enough for French - economists.
newsitem.headline: Recent dollar rise not enough for French - economists.

text.p: The dollar's recent sharp rise against European currencies could continue but will probably stop short of levels that the French government is believed to want, economists say.
And as long as Paris insists on keeping the franc pegged to the mark, the Germans will have the ultimate power to decide the dollar's rate in Europe, they add.
"The French want six francs to the dollar or even more, but the question of what they will get depends on the Germans," JP Morgan economist David Naude said.

The Bundesbank could exercise that power by cutting interest rates, but signs that the German economy is expanding make such a move doubtful. Any interest rate cut would be timed for German priorities and not to help France.
"Not for France and not ostensibly for Europe, though that will play a part, but we do think Germany will cut," said Sonja Gibbs, economist at Nomura International.
Under these circumstances, there is little chance that the dollar will climb higher than about 5.40 francs -- about 1.60 marks -- before it runs into official German resistance, economists said.
The franc is currently trading around 5.28 per dollar.
Financial markets were also expected to cool their enthusiasm for dollars at least temporarily because of the suddenness of the unit's climb, they said.

French authorities have said repeatedly that they want a stronger dollar. Prime Minister Alain Juppe said last month the U.S. currency was "chronically" undervalued, giving U.S. firms an unfair advantage.
The government wants the franc to weaken against the U.S. unit to help stimulate growth so France can enter European monetary union in better economic health.
"It is true that the dollar is and remains undervalued against the major European currencies," French government spokesman Alain Lamassore told Europe 1 radio on Wednesday.
At the same time, he said, "We must welcome the fact that in a few days it (the dollar) has gone from five francs to 5.30 francs."

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on November 14, when the dollar was worth about 5.09 francs, that he believed the dollar had room to appreciate. At the time, he noted he had also said this when the dollar was at 5.20 francs.
Analysts said they believed the French would like to see a level closer to six francs per dollar.
Using a franc/mark parity of 3.38, a dollar worth six francs would work out to about 1.77 marks and the Germans would never accept that, economists said.
Germany would baulk at a rate much higher than 1.60 marks to the dollar, which translates to about 5.40 francs per dollar, said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley.
Other economists on Wednesday said Germany might accept a level as high as 1.65 marks to the dollar, but no higher.
The fire under the dollar over the last few days was sparked when Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he had no objection to a stronger dollar.
Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing's prediction that investors would switch assets to dollars as the new single European currency established its credibility also helped the greenback.
New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough echoed Issing 24 hours later at a conference in Hong Kong.
